title: Building a mobile puzzle game with an AI agent: what worked (a design book, a headless engine, millions of bot runs, scripted gameplay videos) and what didn’t
author: Dependent-Issue4584
selftext:
The attached clip was made in Studio, a tool I describe in a sec. It runs a scripted scenario right inside the game engine in the browser and then exports it to MP4. No screen recording needed at all.

https://reddit.com/link/1xzbvxn/video/p2ffq8ytkc2i1/player

I’ve been working on Neon Zen, a small path-building puzzle game for Android, using React Native & Expo. You place tiles on a 5x5 board, and a glowing dot follows the lines you’ve connected. After some moves, the tiles disappear, so the board clears. The game has an endless mode and 'JOURNEY' mode with 70 custom stages (so far).  
  
Nearly all of the code was written by Claude Code and Codex. I focused on deciding what the game should be, how it should look, and testing it. A few choices I made led to interesing results, so here’s what I learned.  
  
**The design book**  
  
The first issue I ran into was design drift. Every session made small 'improvements' to the UI. Within a week, it was turning into a really big mess. To get things back on track, I created single HTML file ('design book') that describes the game’s visual design: mockups of every screen and element, colors, spacing, animation behavior, all organized into numbered sections. All the implementation tickets point to specific sections in this document, and the agent is told to follow the book exactly. If something looks wrong in the book, it should flag the problem to me rather than quietly changing it.  
I had to add two rules along the way. First, mockups communicate intent. They’re not pixel-perfect specs. The agent should only change the elements explicitly named in the implementation task. Without this it would rebuild an entire screen to match a rough sketch. Second, a fixed scale factor between the mockups and the device. Before I set that, about half the UI ended up noticeably too small.  
I think this works especially well for this kind of game. The graphics are simple neon lines, shapes and panels, which are easy to draw directly in HTML and SVG. That means the mockups in the design book look a lot like the real screens. It might not be the same case for a 3D game, since a web page probably can’t really show what the player sees. A 2D game built with sprites might work better. You could use the actual sprites in the book to create realistic-looking screens, though I haven’t tried it.  
  
**Keeping the engine separate from the view**  
  
The game logic is pure TypeScript, with no React imports, and it uses a seeded random generator. Each player action evaluates a new state and returns a list of events. The rendering layer just plays those events back. I did this originally so the agent could write tests for every rule and reproduce any bug from a seed. The bigger benefit showed up later. Because the engine doesn’t need a screen, the agent could write a script that runs the game headlessly with a bot, as many times as I want. Each run could use a different stage layout, bot skill level, seed, and set of equipped boosts. A typical test suite that tests few dozen stage variations ran 4 to 9 million rounds, taking approx 2-3 hours.  
  
I used those results to re-balance the 'JOURNEY' stages, and a few results surprised me. Some goals I’d expected to be challenging (like reaching a certain combo or closing a complex loop around obstacles) turned out to be easy even for a dumb bot, so I reworked them. The bots also discovered edge cases in the engine long before any human tester would have.  
  
If you’re starting a logic / puzzle game with an AI agent, I’d separate the logic from the view from day one. It costs very little at the start, and later, questions like 'is this level too hard?' become something you can actually measure. But the bots weren’t the only useful thing to come out of this...  
  
**A studio for gameplay videos**

The same separation paid off when I needed short clips for social media. Recording actual gameplay and hoping for a good-looking fragment of the game was taking too long, so I asked the agent build a small tool I call Studio. It runs in the browser using the real game engine and renderer. I (or the AI agent) write a scenario: the starting board, the tiles that appear in the player's hand, and the sequence of actions. Then the game plays itself exactly as written. I can preview it, adjust the details, and export the result as an MP4 file.  
  
The best part is that every scenario is defined as JSON file. If I change a skin or an effect, I simply re-export the scenarios, and every video reflects the current look of the game. It also works the other way - if a scenario looks bad on screen, that's usually a sign the actual moment feels bad in the game too.  
  
The video at the top of this post was made in the Studio.  
  
**What was my role?**  
  
Mostly, it came down to taste. The agent can handle the tasks like 'implement §14 from the design book', but it can’t tell whether the game feels calm or just slow. Game feel, sound timing, and deciding which ideas to cut were still my job. I keep a list of rejected mechanics so the same ideas don’t keep coming back. The same goes for performance on a real mid-range phone. I recently spent a lot of time on rendering improvements because the code the agent wrote was correct but too heavy for some of the devices.  
  
I’m curious how others approach the design phase. How do you keep visuals consistent across many AI sessions, especially with sprites or 3D, where an HTML mockup isn't enough?
